utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I think there is nothing to discuss before the witness enters the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone, Mr. Butler. Could we start with P125.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we are waiting: We are still on the topic of prisoners and documents and materials specifically related to General Tolimir and that subject. We had just talked about the document from General Tolimir, where he briefly mentioned the able-bodied men being evacuated, in his words, from Potocari, and we had a brief discussion of a Popovic document on that same topic. And now continuing on the topic of prisoners, and we now see a document that the Court has seen many times, so I hope not to spend too much time with it. It's the 13 July proposal from General Tolimir and from Borike, at 1400 hours, which we all know is in the Zepa area, and it's to the commander of the Main Staff - I'm sure we'll all agree that's General Mladic - and for his information, the assistant commander for Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs of the Main Staff. Can you remind us who that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May there be peace on this house, and may these proceedings end according to God's will. The Prosecutor said that I was the one who sent this document. Could the Prosecutor please give us a reference, because I'd like us to be able to see from the document, itself, whether it was, indeed, me who sent this document, or, in the alternative, if Mr. McCloskey cannot confirm this, then this should be stricken out of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a misunderstanding. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. If I said "sent" in the terms of actually sending it, that would have been incorrect. It would have been more correct to say that this was a proposal from General Tolimir to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see, in the transcript, page 2, lines 5 to 6: "... it's the 13th July proposal from General Tolimir and from Borike, at 1400 hours ..." That was the relevant sentence. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecutor again said that this was General Tolimir's proposal to General Mladic. Could he tell us on the basis of what he claims this, and whether Tolimir signed any of this, and whether there is any document confirming that this was, indeed, the case? Otherwise, it should be just deleted out of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the general is very familiar with the Prosecution's position on this, and I really -- and we know he's questioning the authenticity, but I'm just talking about, right now, the document, on its face. And we can see, on its face, that it's to the commander of the Main Staff, and it's saying, on the fourth line in the English "assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff proposes the following measures:" So really what I'm doing is, I'm just saying we see this document, it's dated the 13th, it's to Mladic, it's a proposal from the assistant commander for security and intelligence. I hadn't gotten to that part yet, but I was going to ask Mr. Butler to tell us who the assistant commander for morale was, or remind us. And if it's going to be an issue, I can ask him who the assistant commander for security and intelligence is. So we're just talking about the document. I think the Court is fully aware of the authenticity arguments. It's not something I really intended to go into with this witness in any great degree. I just want to get some of the basic information that's in it and ask Mr. Butler about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all recall that Witness Savcic testified about this document, and it was his position that he didn't sign this or a similar document, if I'm not mistaken in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct, and no one is suggesting that anyone signed this. I would, of course, take you back to the witness whose initials are on this as the person who sent it and who identified their inked initials on the original to go into that subject. But, really, that subject of authenticity, inked originals, who signed what, wide open for cross-examination, but I think I -- I didn't want to get into that with this witness on this document. We've got many more to go, so I hadn't gotten there with him, and I didn't really intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are referring now to Witness Gojkovic. There was some dispute if there was a forward command post, IKM, at this location. But, nevertheless, we have the document in front of us, and I think the Prosecutor may use this document in putting it to the witness and asking questions. We don't know yet the questions. You should wait for what kind of questions he will put to the witness, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no problem with the Prosecutor putting questions to the witness the entire day about this document, but he should not premise it with the words that this is a document coming from the assistant commander because this is a document from an unauthorised source. And we've shown here -- we've proven that it's not an authentic document, that it didn't go through the coded messages system, and I believe that we need to have an expert who can actually speak to the handwriting on the document, itself, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the position of the Defence in relation to this document, you may take this into account as you, of course, do, and please continue your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you remind us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I gave now the floor to Mr. McCloskey. Your position is clear on the record. The position of the Prosecution is also on the record. I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey to continue with his questions. There is no need to repeat your position. We have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not wish to repeat my position here. I just would like the Trial Chamber to order that that portion of the transcript, where it says -- where General Tolimir's name is mentioned, and saying that it's his proposal, I would just like that to be deleted out of the transcript because it's not true. I would like what is not true to be deleted from the transcript, because if it cannot be proven by any documents or in any other manner, then it's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you know that the transcript is a clear reflection of what was said in the courtroom, and Mr. McCloskey said that, notwithstanding if that was true or not. Your name is not mentioned in this document. That is very clear, that is his assumption, but we cannot delete anything from the record. It's a clear reflection of what was said in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To make a long story short, I would like to read this relevant part of the document into the record. I quote: "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS proposes the following measures:" It's clear that the name of Mr. Tolimir is not included in this document, and, Mr. McCloskey, I would kindly ask you to rephrase your question. But it was not a question yet. You have put something on the record, and then you wanted to put a question which was not answered yet. Mr. Tolimir, it is technically not possible and it would be against our Rules to delete anything from the transcript. The transcript is a clear reflection also of different statements in the courtroom. They may be correct or not correct, but we can't delete anything. Mr. McCloskey, please continue. We all agree that the name of Mr. Tolimir is not mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, I think the general's thinking that I am making some kind of a conclusion here or some sort of analysis, when, in fact, I'm just fundamentally repeating what is in the document. And I'm sure General Tolimir is not challenging that he or someone else is the assistant commander for security and intelligence, but I -- and -- but I will take, of course, all of that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Butler, can you remind us, if you know, who the assistant commander for Morale, Religious and Legal Affairs for the Main Staff is, the second person in this address on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That individual would be General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the next person on the list of addressees is commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. Do you recall who that was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That commander was Major Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see in the first paragraph that there is a reference that says: "There are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). Prisoners are under the control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment." These over 1.000 members referred to here in this document, of the 28th Division, where, in your view, are they coming from, and who are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These particular individuals would be those members of the column who were either captured by or surrendered to the army and police forces along the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In the next line we see: "Assistant commander for Security and Intelligence Affairs of the GS VRS proposes the following measures:" Who was the assistant commander for Security and Intel Affairs of the Main Staff in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be General Tolimir, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And given that this statement says the "assistant commander for Security and Intelligence Affairs," et cetera, "proposes the following measures," and then we see four measures: Militarily, if General Tolimir is making this proposal, would this document be an indication that General Tolimir was aware of the 1.000 prisoners referred to in the first line of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of any process by which an officer makes a proposal to his superior, that officer is expected to have some knowledge of the situation in order to make the most intelligent proposals possible. It doesn't do a commander or a decision-maker any service to have proposals which aren't grounded in reality sent to him for his potential decision. So in this context, he knows about the number of prisoners and their location as well as the impacts of -- that these prisoners at that location might have on other potential issues which he addresses in the specifics of the things that he is proposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If General Tolimir is, in fact, in the area of Borike or the Zepa theatre at around 1400 hours, as we see in this document, why would he be dealing with issues related to Srebrenica Muslims if he is dealing with issues related to Zepa, which I think he'll agree the 13th was the day before the major attack on Zepa, which was the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, as a general and the assistant commander for Security and Intelligence of the Main Staff, General Tolimir is going to have the ability to multitask. These are issues, as they are occurring on the 13th of July, that are of some significance not only to the Drina Corps, but to the army, in general. The idea that General Tolimir could only focus on a narrow aspect of Zepa, to the exclusion of military events happening in other areas of the country, doesn't seem to be, you know, within the context of his job as the overall head of Intelligence and Security for the army. He wouldn't set those duties aside just to focus on one particular function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we look at - and I won't go over all of them, the Court's seen them - the four points of this document, are they consistent with his job as assistant commander for Security and Intel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to points 1, 2 and 3 -- I'm sorry, points 1 and 2, those would be completely consistent with his position. Point 3, given the fact that the document is entitled and it is signed by Colonel Savcic seems to be a point that Colonel Savcic, as the superior of Major Malinic, would be directing the Military Police Battalion commander, as is point 4, where he's telling the battalion commander who receives the order to make contact with other individuals and then verify that the proposals have been accepted. So in this context, you see General Tolimir's giving out proposals which were in line with his position, and the actual commander of the 65th Protection Regiment giving orders to his subordinate, which is in line with his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the commander of the Military Police Battalion? It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. That would be Major Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell from this document who made the comment or proposal or order to -- in number 3, to -- and referring -- it says: "... shall take measures to remove the war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road," and the part I'm asking you about is "place them somewhere indoors or an area protected from observation from the ground or the air." Now, if this is a proposal, who, if you can tell, would have made this proposal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, with regard to point 3, I don't know that I read that as a proposal. It inflects that the commander of the Military Police Battalion shall take measures directive in nature, so in the context I would say that that point 3 would be directed by Colonel Savcic, as Major Malinic's immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And would -- in the context of this document, should -- let me say: Should General Tolimir have been aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And given the context, if he is aware of the order, can you give your interpretation on whether or not he would have agreed with that order or approved it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since these first two -- since, first, the document is titled "Dealing with procedures for treatment," and points 1 and 2 deal with prohibiting access particularly to unauthorised individuals filming and photographing prisoners, point 3 would be consistent with that earlier guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But my question is: Should General Tolimir have approved -- would he have approved this order from Savcic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that it's -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that it is consistent with his guidance, I would say yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these questions and answers, based on a document not signed by Savcic, not recognised by Savcic, so a document by an imaginary author to the chief of staff, are being asked by Mr. McCloskey in the form of hypothetical questions, Would he approve? How can we know whether I would or would not approve something that was not signed? And a Prosecution witness said here before the Court that he did not sign it. I kindly ask you to disallow these hypothetical questions that are not based on any real grounds, not to allow speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document, as you'll recall, is in court. You have seen the original. It was part of the Drina Corps collection, as you'll recall, from Tomasz Blaszczyk's testimony. Danko Gojkovic testified that on this document were his inked initials, and that, while he didn't remember this document in particular, this meant that this document was something that he would have sent over the telecommunications system. We have had an expert that has found other typewritten documents and found that this particular document matched those typewritten documents, so if this is some forgery, there are other forgeries from the same typewriter. It's the position of the Prosecution that this is an absolutely genuine document reflecting a genuine proposal. And I completely understand the general and why he is challenging this, and that he is challenging it, as is his right, but there is certainly a firm foundation from this document that is in evidence that it is real and true. And the fact that in wartime someone doesn't sign a document or someone puts their name in place of someone else when they're asking for a proposal, you've heard evidence on that. Things like this happen in war. It's our view that this is absolutely genuine and these questions are appropriate. This is an argument for a later day, in my view, but since the general has made it, I'm giving you mine. But I think there is certainly enough genuine, solid evidence for Mr. Butler to give us his military view on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not interpreting your lines of questions as a way to authenticate this document. I understand your line of questions in a different way: that you try to find out the areas of responsibility of certain members of the VRS, in relation to possible orders reflected in such a document, who would be responsible for certain orders. The Chamber is aware of the fact that there are different testimonies of witnesses in relation to this document; Witness Malinic, Witness Gojkovic, Witness Savcic. It is for the Chamber to decide, at the end of the day, if anybody can rely on this document or not. This is not the day to do that now. Discussing speculation, you could say, Mr. Tolimir, that every answer from this witness is speculation because he was not an eye-witness and he was not on the ground. He provides his testimony, and we have to be aware of this fact, on the basis of studying material. This is the basis of his expert opinion which is used by the Prosecution. And, Mr. Tolimir, you have every right to challenge the testimony, and you will have the opportunity, during your cross-examination, to do that also in relation to this document or in relation to the answers given by this witness in relation to the content of this document. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we see again from the document that there is a time on it, 1400 hours, in the top left, and at the bottom it says: "Delivered at 1510 hours." This would be the 13th of July, and it's, of course, talking about over 1.000 prisoners at Kasaba. Are you aware, from your knowledge of the investigation, whether or not by the evening of 13 July there were more prisoners in the area from Nova Kasaba along the road towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm aware from the investigation that through the course of the day, the number of prisoners that were being captured between Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje and further down towards Bratunac, including Sandici, by the end of that day probably numbered at least 2.000, and on subsequent days those numbers increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, in reviewing and studying and analysing this document, did you find any documents by General Mladic that you felt were related to this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shortly after these proposals are made, there is a document from the Main Staff, under the signature of General Mladic, where those various -- I believe it's under the signature of General Mladic. I'm not sure if it's personally his or -- or perhaps just another officer at this juncture, but where these proposals are, in fact, accepted, some of them are modified, and orders are sent out to subordinate formations of the Drina Corps and other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P655, the next tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This document, we see, is dated 13 July, and we see a "Received" stamp of 2250 hours, 13 July, up in the right-hand corner. And if we look at the -- well, we can look at the original B/C/S and see that it's in the name of Commander Colonel General Ratko Mladic, and that stamp is dated the 14th of July. Now, in your view, in taking a look at this document entitled "Preventing leakage of military secrets in the area of combat operations - order," and it says: "In order to ensure the organised conduct of planned combat operations and other activities in the general sector of Srebrenica and Zepa, and in order to prevent the leakage of confidential information classified as military secrets, I hereby order:" And then various things. Is this, in your view, at all related to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on what do you base that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one were to look at the actual steps of the order, it discusses which various roads, for example, in points 2 and 3, which various roads are to be closed, except for military and police traffic, where check-points are to be set up, and point 5 discussing a ban on giving out any information on activities in that area, particularly related to prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, escapees and similar, so I believe that these particular directions are, to a large degree, based on the recommendations of General Tolimir, as outlined in that last order we discussed or last document we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, which is the same time-frame, but I just want to ask you briefly something about it. It is 65 ter 43. It should be under tab 21, another 13 July document with a stamp at the back of 1335 hours. But it is, as we can see, from the Main Staff, and it's to the Command of the Drina Corps and the various brigades, entitled "Order to prevent the passage of Muslim groups towards Tuzla and Kladanj." And we see that it describes what is now familiar facts to us; the Muslims going through the area and, as we can see, an order to engage people, to protect the Serbian area, to capture the disarmed Muslims -- to capture and disarm Muslims, et cetera. I won't go into the detail. We get to number 7, which is page 2 in the English. It's a note that says: "Use secure channels to communicate information about captured or blocked groups." And then number 8: "Send interim reports with specific details of the situation in the area of responsibility of all units so that the corps command and Main Staff can act in a timely manner." And this is in the name of Assistant Commander Lieutenant General Milan Gvero. Now, what, if anything, can you make of the fact that General Gvero is sending this direction -- or, excuse me, order? It's actually entitled "Order."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've discussed in earlier testimony, those senior officers who are performing their duties are not going to be issuing orders that are outside of their particular competence to issue. In this particular case, you know, General Gvero, for whatever reason, has obviously been empowered, presumably by General Mladic, to issue this order. It may very well be, in part, that at the time, with the absence of General Milovanovic, he is the senior official at the Main Staff, assuming at this time General Mladic isn't there and General Miletic may or may not be otherwise occupied, so General Gvero could give out this order. I take it the fact that General Gvero has issued the order, and that the order is properly accepted by the subordinate units, that at the time it was issued no one questioned whether or not General Gvero was authorised to make such an instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where would this order indicate that General Gvero was at the time it was made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would indicate that he's at the physical location of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we assume, for the purpose of this question, that on the evening of -- or, excuse me, the afternoon of 13 July, that General Mladic is still in the Bratunac/Srebrenica area, and General Tolimir is in the Zepa/Borike area, and General Milovanovic is in the -- out in the West Krajina area, does that fit with your conclusion or counter it in some way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that is very consistent with what I've indicated. For example, on the 9th and 10th of July, General Gvero was at the IKM at Pribicevac to, in part, take a look at what was happening with the Srebrenica operation. The pattern of the Main Staff sending its generals to various combat locations to do -- and observe various issues is one that is seen throughout the conflict. From a command-and-control perspective, it certainly is a prudent practice. So, I mean, I don't see anything inconsistent about that at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this 65 ter 43 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 43 shall be assigned Exhibit P2487. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now staying on our topic of 13 July and prisoners, the location of prisoners, the knowledge of prisoners, if we could go to P4136. Excuse me, that may be a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We haven't received more than 4.000 documents yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, I'm sorry, that's P413B, as in "Bravo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told it's confidential and should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this, as we're getting to it, Mr. Butler, is a 2nd Corps intercept, dated 13 July, at -- we should have the one at 1730 hours. And I believe this is an intercept you're familiar with and have talked about before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted a clarification. At page 17, lines 14 through to 19, you have stated that: "For example, on the 9th and 10th of July, General Gvero was at the IKM to, in part, take part and look at what was happening in the Srebrenica operation." How do you come to know this fact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is one particular document, and I believe it's dated the 9th of July, that is sent to the IKM Pribicevac, and it is addressed to both General Krstic and General Gvero, which reflects General Gvero -- that the people who are sending him that document are aware that he is physically present at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, Your Honours, much of what I'm doing is a chronology of the events, so these documents are there, and I'm sure we'll get to July 9th sooner than later. And, of course, Mr. Butler jumped the chronology slightly, which, of course, is going to happen as he's answering questions. But just to let you know, we will be in the chronology that should help us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So this, we see, is X and Y, and it starts out: "Is it possible for us to send about a dozen buses from Bijeljina?" Then Y says: "Call them to come immediately. There are now about 6.000 of these." And then X says: "Fit for military service." Y says: "Quiet, don't repeat." X says: "All right, then I am to send." And it goes on. We best go over in English on the computer. And it talks about: "Go ahead, send. I have three check-points, fuck. I have the one where you and I were when there is up there where the check-point at the junction is, and there is halfway from the check-point to the boarding point." It goes on to say, Y says: "According to a rough estimate, there are 1500 to 2.000 in each place." X says: "And are they still transporting those women and children?" And it goes on to talk about some information. It mentions that X says, after a few lines: "So I am sending them, and they are to report there in the Kasaba at the back." Then Y says: "They should report to the stadium." Then there's talk about Kundasevic and Radakovic collecting. The last few lines: "Fine. They are to drive away and come back." Y says: "They are to drive until they disappear." X says: "Fine, okay." So let's go back to the beginning. Have you -- in your analysis, did you make any conclusions about what this reference to "6.000 of these" were in this context of where X says "fit for military service," and Y says: "Quiet, don't repeat"? What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The two correspondents on the intercept are discussing their estimates of the number of military-aged Muslim men who are being captured or who are surrendering to the VRS at various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you make out -- well, do you know, from the investigation -- this says that there are -- the first line on the next page in English: "I have three check-points ..." It mentions a check-point at a junction. It mentions Kasaba and a stadium. Can you -- do you recall, were there any assembly points that revealed themselves from the investigation that are all consistent or inconsistent with the comments in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, from my work with the investigation years ago, we were able to note and verify that there was certainly one check-point at the intersection of Konjevic Polje on the Nova Kasaba road, there is a second check-point a few kilometres to the north-west of Bratunac along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, and I believe that there is a third check-point somewhere around where the 65th Protection Regiment's military police unit were. I'm sure of the two check-points along Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. The third one I seem to recall, but it's been a few years since that one. But there were a number of check-points there that were designed to stop civilian traffic from going into the area, so that part is consistent with my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about assembly points for prisoners on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, based on my work with the investigation, I'm aware that on the 13th, prisoners were assembled at the -- on the soccer pitch at Nova Kasaba. There was a smaller assembly of prisoners in Konjevic Polje, at the school location there. There was a large number of prisoners assembled on the meadow at Sandici, and they were later taken down to Privica [phoen]. So, again, those assembly points are consistent with this intercept as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if this intercept and the other evidence in the case is roughly correct that there are now 4.000 to 6.000 prisoners at this time that are being collected, is this information that -- and that goes up from the 13 July proposal that we saw. Would this increased information -- should that go to General Tolimir, the chief of Intel and Security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, given the staggering number of prison ers being captured, I can't see how he would not be notified of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer -- this is in evidence. This has a P number. All right. Let's go now to D49, another document that everyone has seen many times. I know Mr. Butler has. I don't want to deal with it at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But we see here a document that says it's from the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. Remind us the town associated with that brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Rogatica, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that it's in the name of Assistant Commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir, and it's to the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff, to General Gvero personally. Now -- and it's entitled "Accommodation of prisoners of war," which they abbreviate "r/z" and says: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all r/z's from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that space," with a word that we've learned has to do with beds and cots of some sort, "has been arranged for 800 prisoners of war in the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade in Sjemec." Now, we see that General Tolimir has addressed this personally to General Gvero. What, if anything, do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, part of that practice, he knows where General Gvero is and that he's engaged in these types of issues, and he wants to ensure that this particular proposal that he's making goes directly to General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see a stamp dated 2230 hours. Do you recall that at the late evening of 13 July, where most of the known prisoners from Srebrenica were being held?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, based on the investigation and survivor accounts, at that particular time most of the prisoners were being held in either facilities in Bratunac, various schools there or hangars, or they were actually in buses, in trucks, parked in front of other locations where they could be more easily guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in those locations, could any of those individuals in those vehicles or schools be seen from the air?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, when -- I believe, as part of various exhibits that have been tendered in other trials, we've seen overhead imagery of clusters of buses in and around Bratunac on 13 July, so they are readily visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But are the people visible that are being held in those buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that they're looking through the tops of the buses, so I would say, at face value, no, the people would not be visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to, on this same topic, go ahead a few days and ask you some questions about July 17th. And if we could go to P554A. And this is an intercept where it's the Prosecution's position it's from 17 July, 2055 hours, and we see that it talks about Trivic, telephone exchange, Colonel Jankovic. And it starts out and says: "It's Badem." Do you remember what this term "Badem" is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem is the telephonic code word for the Bratunac Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so T says: "Give me Colonel Jankovic." Now, on 17 July, 2050 hours, are there any documents or information that reveal who this Colonel Jankovic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is a document that reflects, when one looks back at 12 and 13 July previously, that Colonel Jankovic is a member of the Main Staff intelligence organ. He is a subordinate of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then C says: "Just a second. Zlatar, the extension is still busy." What is C, first of all, or who is C, if you can tell from this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not exactly clear. It might just be a switchboard operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is Zlatar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatar is the telephonic code-name for the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then the intercept says: "You have the colonel on the line." T says: "Hello." And then now we have J: "Yes, I'm listening." And T says: "Well, Jankovic ..." So under this intercept, who should J be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the correspondents would be Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it says: "Yes?" Jankovic says: "Yes?" T says: "Listen here. Miletic said," and then it's "...," so we don't know what Miletic said." Jankovic says: "Yes." T says: "That you should write what you want to do." Jankovic says: "Yes." T says: "And send it urgently by code up to Tolimir." Now, in this context, who is Tolimir in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Jankovic says: "I'm in no position, man, to write. I'm calling here, and there is ..." And T says: "Listen to what I'm telling you ..." Jankovic says: "All right." T says: "And the commander will decide with Tolimir and send you a --" and I think it may be "reply." So in this context, what is Jankovic being told to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's being directed to make a proposal on how to deal with a particular situation to his superior, General Tolimir, and that General Tolimir, with the commander, will make a decision on how to move forward with a particular course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, who would the commander be in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, keeping in mind this is 2050 hours on the 17th, let's go to the next document, P2168. Actually, could we go to the next page and get the handwritten one to try to avoid an issue. This, we can see, is a typewritten one with Momir Nikolic's name in the bottom. But could we go to the handwritten one, which should be the next one. There we go. And can we see the last page of the handwritten one. All right. And we see the initials down there. Now, can we go to the translation for the handwritten one, if we have it. It should be the next -- I think it's next to this English version, but the next English -- there we go. Okay. That's where we want to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now we do see a written document, and in your knowledge, who is this "RJ"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Colonel Radovan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Radovan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Radoslav. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It won't be the last that any of us make. Now, we see the next day, after that conversation where he was told to write something down, he's now, according to this, written something to the Main Staff of the VRS and the Drina Corps Intelligence and Security Department, called "Situation in the Srebrenica Region." I won't go through all of it, but we see, in point 1, it's talking about the wounded Muslims from the 28th Division that were evacuated by the ICRC, which the Court will remember some evidence on. Number 2 talks about the Dutch Battalion commander sending a message concerning the evacuation of the Dutch. Then number 3 talks about an MSF convoy that arrived on the 18th, but was sent back for procedural reasons; and there's a request that: "Will you please use your influence to see to it that all UN and international organisation transports go via Ljubovija; otherwise, we'll have difficulties providing them with an escort." A logistic request, obviously. And this is what I want to ask you about, the question: "Will you please tell me what stand to take in terms of authorisation for evacuation of the international organisation MSF; in fact, how to deal with the so-called local staff? This also applies to the interpreters of the Military Monitors and UNPROFOR." And it mentions that: "The State Security has passed on to us an opinion that President Karadzic had allegedly abolished all local staff who used to work for UNPROFOR." And Jankovic said: "It is our opinion that they should not be held." First of all, who do you think Jankovic is asking this question to? All we see is it's to the Main Staff, "ObP," the Intelligence and Security Section.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is he is asking General Tolimir for guidance in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you know, do you recall who these MSF people are, the local staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm aware from my work with the investigation that there was some issue related to whether or not the local staff members, those individuals who are Bosnian Muslims but who were working with or in support of both the United Nations observers and the MSF organisation, if they would be permitted to depart when those organisations left Srebrenica after the fall of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether these people were male or female?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a mixed number, but there was some -- there is a listing of them and a number of them are people who would be considered of military age from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So this is a document, and if we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I wonder if you could assist with some clarification. At page 28, line 13/14, you've stated just now that: "My opinion is he is asking General Tolimir for guidance in this situation." I assume, and you may correct me if I'm wrong, that your opinion arises from the document on the screen. And if I'm correct, can you just show us where this reference is made which leads you to this opinion or conclusion? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It's actually a constructive opinion not only based on this document, but based on the prior intercept that was discussed, where the individual correspondents are discussing the fact and Colonel Jankovic gets the guidance that he needs to write up this proposal for General Tolimir. I see the two documents, one exhibit and then the follow-on document, they are linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I take the opportunity to ask you, Mr. McCloskey, about the two different documents, P2168 we have in the binder. We have, of course, the original B/C/S, the handwritten version, but are these two English versions the translations of the handwritten and the typed version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is my understanding, and I believe that because we see the initials of "RJ" on the English version up on the screen, and we see the handwritten initials on the left side, and the other one is -- Momir Nikolic is on both of them. And I know it goes a while back, but you'll remember the testimony of Momir Nikolic on this point. I can recall it -- well, Mr. Butler may remember it as well, which may be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see now that the second English page with the initials "RJ" has, on top, an explanation: "Handwritten document." That clarifies the situation. Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I just -- in going back to Judge Nyambe's question, when this document, entitled "Situation in the Srebrenica Region," when it's specifically addressed to the Main Staff Intelligence and Security Sector, who, in your view, would that be? Who is the Intelligence and Security Sector? Who would be the eyes that would see it when a document like this was sent there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the head of the sector is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that -- did you incorporate that fact into who Jankovic was sending this to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could Mr. McCloskey please ask the witness to clarify whether General Tolimir, on the date as mentioned here, the 18th, was at the Main Staff, and if he did, did he know that this actually reached General Tolimir? On the basis of what is he claiming this? Is that just another supposition of his?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are always two possibilities, Mr. Tolimir. You may put these questions during your cross-examination, because it's the right of Mr. McCloskey to put the question in a way he wants to do it. Or Mr. McCloskey may do it in accordance with your advice, but it's up to Mr. McCloskey to decide. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, on the general's point -- no, I think I'll wait a few questions. I don't want to lose my train of thought on these documents, and we'll come back to the general's concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could now go to 3070D. That's a 65 ter. It's an intercept -- excuse me, that's 3070A. In the English, 3070 -- sorry, in the B/C/S, 3070A will do it. And I want to go -- it's at the bottom there, between X and Y, and it's the position of the Prosecutor that this is 18 July at 1617 hours and that there are -- the intercept documents show this, but I won't spend the time to do all that again. It's been done. And it says: "Y says that MSF appeared on the bridge with a permit to go to the UNPROFOR base to evacuate the personnel." "X says they cannot go through until they've checked with Toso, 'who are they going to treat there'."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who, in your view, is this Toso?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that "Toso" is a nickname for General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this short intercept, do you connect it with any of the documents we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects that these two unnamed correspondents have an awareness that there is an issue with the MSF and that before anything can occur, they are awaiting guidance from General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3070A shall be assigned Exhibit P2488. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go to P383A, and this is another intercept. The Court has seen this, and I know Mr. Butler has. It's an intercept that starts off with a note that Jankovic's voice was heard on a certain channel and Colonel Djurdjic was heard at another frequency between channels 3 and 4 at 1432 hours. "Participants: Jankovic and Colonel Djurdjic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you remind us, if you know, who Colonel Djurdjic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurdjic was a Main Staff officer who was the focal point for dealing with the UN and other international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see Djurdjic saying: "Is this Jankovic?" And Jankovic says: "Speaking." Djurdjic says: "Hello." Jankovic says: "Speaking." Djurdjic identifies himself as: "Colonel Djurdjic speaking." They go on for a bit. Djurdjic refers to him as "Janko." And then as we go down the page a little bit, Djurdjic said: "Regarding what you were asking." Jankovic says: "Yes." "The boss has ordered that they be halted." And then we go down and we see more information regarding Kristina Smit, a nurse that can go, and a person named Daniel O'Brian, a physician. And it goes on, which I will ask you about as it goes on, but what do you think they are beginning to talk about here in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This intercept discusses the authorisation for at least some members of the MSF organisation that was there in Srebrenica to be given permission to depart the former enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this have anything to do with the previous documents that you've spoken of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is -- this document -- or this particular intercept is related to the previous documents and intercepts that I've discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So they continue to talk. Djurdjic, at the bottom of the page, says: "You hear me well?" Jankovic says: "I can hear you." Then let's go to the next page in the English, and I think we need to go to the next page in the Serbian as well. Djurdjic says: "And only women and children can go. Understand?" Jankovic says: "And what about these young men?" Djurdjic says: "Others. No." Then he says: "I don't know. They might require the whole group to go." Now, I'm sorry, but if we could just go back to the first page again. I wanted to put in that context to get your opinion on that line in the middle of the page, when Djurdjic said: "Regarding what you were asking." Jankovic says: "Yes." And Djurdjic says: "The boss has ordered that they be halted." Can you tell who Djurdjic is referring to when he says "the boss"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, when we see the phrase "the boss" in intercepts, it refers to the appropriate-level commander. So in this particular context, I would say that "the boss" would probably be a reference to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to the second page, where Djurdjic, as we've noted, says: "Others. No." And then he says: "I don't know. They might require the whole group to go." Jankovic -- all we get from there is an "E." Djurdjic says: "Say again." Jankovic says: "That they will require, but they have the government's permission for all of them to go." Now, do you relate -- what do you believe that this comment from Jankovic: "They have the government's permission for all of them to go"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you go down, in the context of the intercept it makes it clear that there's a potential discrepancy between what Colonel Jankovic has heard from -- or is hearing now from the army versus what he's heard previously from civilian organs of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so as we go down there, and we see Djurdjic is getting upset, he swears, and he says: "Can we do this through the girl? I have to ask her to act as mediator here, and now I -- we can't, we can't, we're having a one-way conversation." Jankovic says: "Listen." Djurdjic says: "Yes." Jankovic says: "So they have permission from the Koljevic government?" And Djurdjic says: "Yes." Can you remind us who the Koljevic government is a reference to, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the civilian government of the RS at the time. I'm not exactly sure how that places in with Karadzic as the supreme commander, but Koljevic is a high-ranking member of the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, do you want me to finish this intercept up - I've noticed it's break time - or would you like to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It depends on the minutes you need for finishing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe five, at the most, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's better to have a break. Then you are not under time pressure. We must have our first break now, and we will resume in half an hour, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, sorry, but I have to take you back again to the document behind tab 25, P2168. Do you have any explanation -- perhaps we dealt with that in the courtroom at an earlier stage. I don't recall. We have the B/C/S handwritten version and the typed version. The handwritten version has, at the end, "RJ," and the typed version, and this is reflected in the translations as well, the name "Captain Momir Nikolic." I think Mr. Nikolic testified about that. Can you just explain for today how you see this difference between "RJ" and "Captain Momir Nikolic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I recollect back to the testimony of Momir Nikolic, who, in my recollection, says that Radoslav Jankovic comes to the Bratunac Brigade around the 8th, 9th, or 10th and takes up residence in Momir Nikolic's office to do his work, and that Momir Nikolic, when shown these documents, testified, basically, that this was a handwritten document, the one with the initials, by Radoslav Jankovic that was taken to the Communications Centre, and the Communications Centre, when typing it up on the teleprinter, put Momir Nikolic's name because that's what they were used to doing. And so it went out under Momir Nikolic's name, but it was a document that was drafted by Radoslav Jankovic. And that's at T -- transcript 12434 through 12435. So that's the -- my recollection, that's the fundamental reason why we -- why we see it the way we see it, according to Momir Nikolic, which is the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for reminding me. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would also say that Radoslav Jankovic is not on the Prosecution witness list, but I believe he does reside in Serbia. All right. Now, we're -- we should be still at the page 2 of the English of this document. We just -- he just described the Koljevic -- we need to go back to the intercept, which should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the middle of the page, we see that Jankovic says they have permission from the Koljevic government, who you'd mentioned was, I believe, a member of the -- it's page 2 in both. Okay. So Jankovic says they have permission from the Bosnian Serb government, according to what your knowledge is. Then Djurdjic says: "Yes." Jankovic says: "That they can all go, they have a list." Djurdjic says: "Yes, I know, but ... here, man, I can see the names of a certain Abdulah Kurtovic, Ibrahim Ibrahimovic ...." Are those male or female names, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe those are male names, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then they go on and Jankovic says: "Yes." And then Djurdjic says: "Muhidin Husic, Muhamed Hasic, Masic, Sahin Talovic, Hajrudin Kurtic, Omer Talovic." "Yes." And Djurdjic says: "Two, four, six, seven men." Jankovic says: "Yes, they are taking them as local staff, and they have the permission from Karadz ... Koljevic." Djurdjic says: "All right --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Slow down. Some parts of your reading is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Djurdjic says: "All right. They have the permission, but you know that the procedure you, too, took part in ..." Jankovic says: "Great." Djurdjic says: "Pardon?" Jankovic: "Great, if that's your position, it's good." Now Djurdjic says: "The procedure is such, God damn it, that it should be checked whether those who ... are they able-bodied or older than 60?" And Jankovic says: "They are able-bodied." Djurdjic says: "They are?" Jankovic says: "Yes." We need to go to the next page in English. Djurdjic says: "So that's the procedure. And you saw what you left behind in Bratunac the other day." Jankovic says: "Okay." Djurdjic says: "Am I right?" Jankovic says: "Okay." Then Djurdjic says: "And they, if they agree, let them go in their vehicles and take those women and children." And I'll ask you about the rest of this a bit later. But what, in your view, is Djurdjic and Jankovic talking about when they're mentioning these Muslim names and Djurdjic is asking if they're able-bodied, older than 60?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what had been occurring in the previous days, there was a process in place where, as men were coming into the custody of the army and police at various locations, if they were considered to be able-bodied, those between, roughly, 15 and 60, they were detained. If they were children, if they were older than 60, if they were infirm, they were then allowed to board buses and trucks and be transported out of the enclave. So this is the process that I believe that they are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when Djurdjic says: "So that's the procedure," what, in particular, do you think he's talking about in relation to these able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The separation of the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those men that were separated on 12 and 13 July from their families in Potocari, what, as the investigation revealed, happened to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were subsequently placed on buses and trucks and sent to the Zvornik Brigade area, where they were -- or almost all of them were executed in the subsequent days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue on after Djurdjic confirms: "So that's the procedure. And you saw what you left behind in Bratunac the other day." What do you think this reference "and you saw what you left behind in Bratunac the other day" -- what, if anything, to your knowledge, was left behind in Bratunac, in the context of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the men were separated, starting the 12th and 13th, they were -- after their separation in Potocari, they were then placed into schools and other facilities in Bratunac. Those were the men left behind. Those people who did not fit the criteria of able-bodied men were allowed to be removed from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I made reference to the comment about "vehicles, take those women and children." There's a reference to a little orphan. Jankovic talks about two elderly persons. Djurdjic says -- or it says: "Yes. Two elderly, let them go, let the elderly go." Jankovic says: "Okay." And then Djurdjic says: "Let the elderly go, and tonight, when Toso arrives, you and him must make sure you consult some more, please." Who do you believe Toso is in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Jankovic says: "All right, I will. When is Toso coming?" And Djurdjic says: "In the early evening." Now, can you tell, from these references to Tosomir [phoen] -- General Tolimir, where he is arriving to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of who's saying it, it could be the Main Staff headquarters is what they're referring to, but it is not evidently clear whether they're referring to General Tolimir arriving at the Main Staff headquarters or Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to P2222. If this could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is, again, a confidential document. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And out of an abundance of caution, could we go into private session for just a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 4044. This may help with the question that General Tolimir had earlier about 18 July, as we see that we have a document from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army, Intelligence and Security Sector, 18 July, titled "Intelligence Information." And if we could go to page 4 of the English, and I think it's page 3 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that it is in the name of General Tolimir, and it's drafted by someone with the initials -- I believe that's "MS." Do you recall who that drafter might be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe those initials correspond to Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this -- and I think we can all just, as we flip through it, see that it's a detailed intel report about Muslim forces from various areas around Bosnia, including, on page 3 of the English, parts of the 28th Muslim Division had pulled out from Srebrenica and deployed in the wider area of Zivinice. I won't go into all this, but does this provide you any guidance at all whether -- about the locations of General Tolimir at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It tends to provide additional weight to my view that at the time he's at the Main Staff headquarters, versus Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to continue on this topic where we have General Tolimir involved, according to the Prosecution, with prisoner issues, issues of MSF staff and others. And can we go to P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask one question, please. Page 3 of the English, there's one short form which is "NDH," the last paragraph, and also the longer paragraph in the middle. Mr. Butler, do you know what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not. I believe it is initials relating to territory related to Croatia, but I can't give you the exact translation of those initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that document, 65 ter 4044, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4044 shall be assigned Exhibit P2489. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could have P2187 up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for it: We see that this is the Main Staff of the VRS, Sector for Intelligence and Security, dated 29 July, saying "Very Urgent," to the IKM of the Drina Corps, personally to General Krstic, and Intelligence and Security at the Command of the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, and personally to Colonel Rajko Kusic and Captain Pecanac. Can you remind us who Rajko Kusic is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic is the commander of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it's entitled "Disarmament of the 1st Zepa Brigade." And if we could go to page 2 in the English. We can see, at the top of the page, they're talking about exchange of prisoners. It should be that first page in the Serbian. The paragraph I want to ask you about, and we've seen this before, General Tolimir says: "Continue combat operations in order to surround and destroy the 1st Zepa Brigade until the Muslims make the exchange and carry out the agreement from 24 July related to their disarmament and surrender. Take all necessary measures to prevent them from leaving the encirclement. Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire and do not report them to international organisations. We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." Mr. Butler, are you aware of any military reason or any reason from the documents or materials of this case that would justify this line, this direction: "Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire and do not report them to international organisations"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does the next line, how do you -- can you explain the next line? "We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement." The first question: Are there any Muslim -- any prisoners that can be exchanged that have not been registered with the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one goes back to some of the previous documents that we discussed, it makes it clear that General Tolimir's understanding is that some individuals who haven't been registered aren't open to be exchanged in the earlier years, 1993/1994. If you're going to exchange prisoners of war, you're going to do so, you have to have them at least registered, at a minimum, with international organisations, such as the Red Cross, so you can identify them and their numbers to start laying out your negotiating position as to how many you have captured and how many you wish to exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what can you make, if anything, from this two sentences? First, he says, Do not register persons, and then he says, We're going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims don't carry out their agreement or break through.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appear to be contradictory sentences. There's no logical reason why you would not want to do it unless the goal was to keep the prisoners, list them so you're aware of who they are, but deny that same information to international organisations so they wouldn't know how many prisoners you actually had captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document related to this issue. This document, I see, does not have a previous 65 ter number. The one we now have is 7438, 7438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to use -- to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection to any document that would confirm the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Leave is granted to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I won't read all this. We can look at it ourselves. We're not there yet. It should be on one page of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should be 65 ter 7438.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart tells me somehow it didn't get into e-court, but I hope it's in everyone's binders on tab 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should proceed on that basis, and we hope that it will be up-loaded into e-court soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can put the B/C/S on the ELMO. I'm not sure if the Defence has this. Does the Defence have this document? If they do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic is nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we can see that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you could give a hard copy of both versions, English and B/C/S, to the Registry if you are going to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I planned on that, and I will do that, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid I don't have a printed copy of the document Mr. McCloskey intends to use. I would be grateful if he could just identify the document in some way. I have some documents that are not numbered. If he could just remind us what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document is in the binder we all received, behind tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. There is no document behind tab 31 in my binder. That's why I'm on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In our binder, it's a document from the 1st Krajina Corps Command, signed by a certain Momir Talic. The date of this document seems to be the 26th of August, 1995. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just found it among my copies, so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I see that you have that in front of you. We haven't heard a lot about the 1st Krajina Corps and General Talic. Can you just brief us, what you believe this document's about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps is -- was one of the six combat corps of the Army of the Republika Srpska. General Talic at the time was the corps commander. This particular document lays out General Talic's awareness that a number of -- first, a number of Krajina Corps members had been captured in the past and were in the custody of the ABiH, and that his corps does not have enough captured ABiH members in order to effect a trade for these prisoners. So based on his knowledge that they are capturing runaway groups of Muslim soldiers from Zepa and Srebrenica, and the interests in the Tuzla Prisoner Commission to exchange for these types of soldiers, General Talic is asking the chief of staff of the Drina Corps if certain prisoners from Zepa and Srebrenica can be transferred to the custody of the 1st Krajina Corps so these prisoners can then be subsequently transferred and exchanged for VRS prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7438 shall be assigned Exhibit P2490. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on, later in the year on this same topic, to P2250, which, as we're waiting for it, you'll see under tab 32 is another document from the Main Staff Intel and Security Sector, dated 3 September, and it's to many of the corps; not all of them. And it's entitled "Exchange of Prisoners, Report." And if we look at the last page, we see that it's from Assistant Commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir. And I don't want to go through all of this report, but if we go to page 2 in the English, it talks about the Main Staff approved individual exchanges for the 1st KK and East Bosnia commissions on the base of the "one-for-one" principle. And it talks about the Muslims are blocking all exchanges on the "all-for-all" principle and the "one-for-one" principle, making it, and I quote in the third English paragraph: "... making it conditional that a larger number of Muslims from the area of Srebrenica and Zepa be exchanged and the number of Muslims we have in our prisons."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us -- we've heard about this before, but what's going on here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this particular point in time, 3 September, both the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves have long since fallen, and there is an issue between the number of prisoners that the Muslims claim must have been taken versus the number of Muslim prisoners that VRS is claiming that they have possession of in their prisons. So this is the issues that they're trying to negotiate between the various prisoner commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the "one-to-one" and the "all-for-all," and what you recall about how that worked over time, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historically during the conflict, the VRS captured less prisoners than the ABiH side did. As a result, when one looks at the documents from 1993, 1994, and early 1995, prior to Srebrenica, the VRS position was an "all-for-all" exchange, that both sides would essentially swap the amount of -- all of the prisoners that they had, in which case it didn't matter that the VRS had a lesser number of prisoners. The Muslim side, for their part, trying to maximise the number of people they got back, had always pushed more for a "one-for-one" exchange, knowing they had more prisoners. Post July 1995, you start to see switch-overs of that position primarily because the Muslims believe now that the Bosnian Serb side has a far greater number of prisoners from both Srebrenica and Zepa than the Muslims are holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go to page 4 in the English. It should be the last page in the B/C/S, above this signature block. It should be the third paragraph up in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I want to call your attention to the sentence that begins: "The Exchange Commission chairman must view the exchange proposal integrally, as does the Main Staff of the VRS, since so far the Main Staff has made the necessary number of prisoners available for the Corps Commissions in circumstances where they did not have a sufficient number of captured enemy soldiers to exchange for all the captured members of their corps. Security organs and Exchange Commission chairmen must also avoid using parents' bitterness because it is not possible to exchange prisoners who have been in prison for quite some time, particularly because the GS VRS is not responsible for this situation, rather it is the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our units." Now, General Tolimir says here, basically, that this situation they're in is not the fault of the Main Staff, but rather it's the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by "our units."
