If we go back to the document of 13 July, where, in the document under Savcic's name, the assistant commander for Intel and Security is mentioned, and there is an acknowledgment of over 1.000 prisoners in the area of Kasaba. There is also an acknowledgement in General Tolimir's 12 July document of able-bodied Muslim men being "evacuated," in quotes, from Potocari. And if we take into account the prisoners captured along the road near Kravica, Konjevic Polje, how do you explain, if you can, General Tolimir saying that it's the "result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our units"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the other corps units, it is a sense of frustration and admonishment that he's telling those corps that, You haven't captured enough people to make favourable exchanges with people from your own corps that have been captured. In the case of the Drina Corps, which General Tolimir obviously is aware has captured thousands of prisoners, I'm not sure how the Drina Corps would possibly take that or how the other corps take it, given the fact that they, too, are aware of thousands of prisoners who had been taken by the Drina Corps from Srebrenica alone and they're now not available for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go into a little bit of a different area. Those were the areas specific to General Tolimir and prisoner issues that I wanted to lead with for this testimony. If we could now go to 65 ter 397. It should be on the next tab, and we'll see that it's entitled "Analysis of the Combat Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska, 1992," and it's dated April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend a whole lot of time on this, Mr. Butler, but is this a document that you have reviewed and analysed and speak about in your various reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 83 in the English, B/C/S page 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see this is the section of -- can you basically tell us, briefly, what this is, this report I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was customary for every unit of the Army of the Republika Srpska, on an annual basis, to do what is essentially a self-evaluation of their combat capabilities and abilities. This particular report represents the analysis that the Main Staff did of their own capabilities for the prior year, 1992. As part of laying out their analysis of their capabilities, where they've performed well, where they've not performed well, the report lays out all of the relative functions that the army and, by definition, the Main Staff manage. This particular section here deals with the functions both under intelligence and security that the Main Staff Sector for Intelligence and Security Support has. It details the issues involved in setting up the various sectors, individuals -- who they're needing to recruit to man these sectors, as well as all of the other problems involved with where they were in 1992, starting an army from, essentially, scratch as well as projecting out how well they've done and where they're going in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get into the intel and security section briefly: Do you recall if there's anything in this document related to the use of Main Staff senior officers at combat fronts? I may have that mixed up with another document. I just -- you had talked about that earlier, and I just wondered if you remembered that at all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, in this particular document, under a section entitled "Command and Control," it does talk about the issue, that it was viewed as a positive that at critical areas of the battle-front Main Staff personnel showed up in order to monitor the situation. As I indicated before, it was a fairly prevalent practice during the war for that to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I know it's getting late, but you said they just showed up. Do you want to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, they are not accidental tourists. They're sent there by the Main Staff, by the Main Staff's commander, in order to monitor the activities that are going on, to synchronise those with the goals and objectives of the Main Staff, to ensure that the corps is handling the situation in the manner that they wish it to be handled. And if there are problems, the physical presence of a Main Staff general there can help deal with any potential de-conflictions or other problems as they arise. It should be noted that when one looks at the combat activities that occur, more often than not it's not just a single corps that is involved. Some of these operations will involve two or even three corps co-ordinating against a single strategic or an operational objective. So having a Main Staff general officer or senior officer at a forward location, forward command post, is very beneficial in being able to ensure that everything is de-conflicted as it needs to be and that the activities of those multiple corps formations are appropriately synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's "de-conflicted" mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a military sense, as part of the orders process, various units, various roads, various objectives are all allocated to the units that are participating in them. Where things can get problematic is that after an operation has commenced, and as forces are moving forward or achieving their objectives, and as new objectives are designated, there will be a certain competition between the military forces as to who can use what roads or who has priority over what ammunition or other resources. So as an operation continues underway, there is a certain amount of de-confliction that has to take place, where the senior headquarters determines what are the primary objectives, which military formation is going to achieve those objectives, and what other military formations are going to support the achievement of those objectives, how much resources that they're going to get, and who is the priority of effort for getting those resources. It's just part of assuring that military operations are undertaken as efficiently and as effectively as possible, given the logistics and other constraints on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's deal briefly with -- we see that we're at the Intel and Security section, "Intelligence Support," paragraph 5.1. Let's go to the next page in English. It's page 75 in the Serbian. Just one line down at the bottom of the page: "The Department for Intelligence and Security Affairs circulated instructions on the interrogation of prisoners of war to the relevant organs in subordinated units." Is this action described here consistent with your knowledge of how the rules should work, that the intelligence unit would be involved in instructions on the interrogations of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page - 76 in Serbian, 85 in the English - just to show that this is the beginning of the security support section. And if we could go to page 88, and page 78 in the Serbian, just in the middle of the page again. Just one sentence I want to ask you about. It reads: "A particular problem, especially at the tactical level, is the leakage of confidential military data by radio communications." So in your view, as early as 1992, what do you think they are concerned with? What is this problem of leakage? How is it leaking?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of a shortage of cryptologic security, keys and equipment, particularly at the lower unit levels, it was recognised very early on that the enemy was gaining valuable intelligence about the VRS and their immediate intentions during operations by listening to individuals talking over lines that are not secure. The obvious easy way to solve that problem is to secure the communications, but in 1992 and throughout the war, the VRS generally did not have access to the equipment necessary to do that. So they had to assume the risk, as it were, of using equipment that was not secured, in light of the fact that they still had to effectively manage command and control of their military formations. So they did their best to education their people that their communications were subject to intercept, but at times of stress or at other periods of times, I mean, it was unavoidable that valuable information would leak to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. And I take it you're only referring to those pages which are included in the binder, starting with page 83 and the cover pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. It is fully translated in English, and if the Defence would like it all in, I have no objection. But I think for our purposes, this should -- this should suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to invite the Prosecution to up-load those parts of this whole document you are really tendering in a separate document, and for today we mark it for identification. It will then be received as a separate document after up-loading.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 397 shall be assigned Exhibit P2491, and that exhibit number is assigned to the whole document containing 142 pages in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not the intention. That wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be only marked for identification, the whole document. And after up-loading the relevant parts, it will be received as a separate document with this number. Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'm still on the topic of intel and security areas and how it works. You've talked a bit about counter-intelligence. Can we go to 65 ter 2224. And this is a document that I know you're familiar with from the 20th of April, 1995, from the Command of the Drina Corps Security Department, under the name of its chief, which is on the second page in English, but I think we can just stay there. We should be able to see it at the bottom of the Serbian, Lieutenant General Vujadin Popovic. And it's to various brigades, we can see, of the Drina Corps. And it says, and I'll just paraphrase: that they have a reliable source that there has been an assassination contracted on General Mladic and General Tolimir, and then it issues various measures. Where, if anywhere, would this kind of work or threat fit into the task of the intel and security branch or organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be a classical counter-intelligence task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell from this whether this is a threat from the enemy or a threat from inside the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, given the context of it occurring after the 50th session of the RS, this is a threat from inside the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see number 4: "The Security Administration has designated this case operative action 'Judas.'" Does that support what you just said, just what they named it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Code-names aren't supposed to give away the actual context of the operation, but certainly in this case it tends to support the idea that various members of the political side of the government might have contracted out the assassination of these two members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, for something to be considered in the realm of counter-intelligence, does it matter whether it's an internal threat, like this document shows, or an external threat from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P2216, and I'm talking about the -- some of the practices of the Security and Intel Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a -- as it will come up, a long document that I don't intend to get into a lot of detail for you. The Court's seen it before. But it's dated 18 March 1995, to the commander of the Main Staff and to the assistant commander for Security and Intelligence of the Main Staff. So that would be - I'm sure there's an agreement - General Mladic and General Tolimir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we're a ways from there and I don't think we need to go to it in the computer, but at the end of this we see that this is in the name of the chief, Colonel Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please wait a moment, because the Registrar is struggling with some problems with the documents. Now we have the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see this document that, apparently, from the face of it, Colonel Beara has written to General Mladic and General Tolimir and to the commands of the -- we see the various corps and others, entitled "Analysis of the Situation in the Military Police Units of the Army of Republika Srpska." And does the -- the various advice, recommendations, comments set forth by Colonel Beara, is that consistent with your understanding of how his job should work in relation to supervising the work of military police forces throughout the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, in fact, if one looks at the English-language version on page 2, it notes that this report follows inspections by -- or of these particular units, and that the results of these inspections, they're now doing an analysis to identify all of the various issues related to the manning, use and employment. These are, again, the typical functions that the security branch would have in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 3 in the English, and it's page -- it should be page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see a handwritten section in this where someone has written in hand addressed to Toso. Would that be the same Toso, the same General Tolimir that you identified earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from the context of this, do you have an opinion on who would be writing to Toso, to Tolimir, like this and saying it's a disgrace to have a soldier commanding a unit after three years and such things, commenting on the report of Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of the particular comments, it would have to be a military officer who's superior to General Tolimir. So that leaves you either General Mladic, as the commander of the Main Staff, or General Milovanovic, as the deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I note, in my review of this document, I did not see any references to the military police and the detention or transportation or the securing of prisoners of war. Would that suggest that the military police would not have those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It simply suggests that within the context of this particular report, that particular -- that particular issue was not considered to be a problem at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I see that that's already in evidence, so let's go now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you go to the next one, I have to come back to 65 ter 2224. This is not in evidence yet you have used before. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for catching that, Mr. President. Yes, I -- it was my intention to, and I just missed it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2224 shall be assigned Exhibit P2492. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm also informed by Ms. Stewart that 65 ter 7438 is now in e-court. I think it was given P2490.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And it has been updated in the e-court. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could now go to P1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Still on the topic of the basic responsibilities of security organs, we see another document from Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, the Drina Corps Command. This is dated 18 July 1995. We see it's to the brigades that we know are part of the Drina Corps, and other units, entitled "Dealing with reporter crews." And it talks about a large number of foreign and domestic reporters expected to come, and how to deal with them. Is this -- does this document reflect, in your view, a normal responsibility for a security officer such as Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 2223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another document from Colonel Popovic of the Drina Corps. This one is 7 February 1995, and we can see he's sending it to the brigades. And it's also entitled -- well, it's entitled "Command of the Military Police," and it has various comments and suggestions in this, and tasks. Does this reflect a normal relationship of a security officer with the military police in the brigades and in his -- and in the corps units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, if one looks at the information that is in that Main Staff report, I suspect one would find that this request for the brigades' military -- to report about their military police, then gets turn around and sent up to the Main Staff and is part of the information they would analyse before making their observations. So this is all part of -- within that military police, part of that technical chain where requests are sent down and information is passed back up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, if this is read carefully, you will not see any references to prisoners of war. Does that have any significance to you relating to whether or not security and MPs would have dealings with prisoners of war in the normal course or as part of their job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, it reflects the fact that particularly this late in the war, there's still a problem, structurally, with the military police of the VRS, in that rather than being allowed to focus on traditional military police tasks, they are still very often being used in a combat environment as a military infantry unit because of shortages of manpower in other units. So as part of identifying, you know, these types of issues, as well as equipment shortages related to the military police, this is all part of an effort by the Main Staff to try and get military police units re-oriented back on their traditional functions rather than have to be used as emergency infantrymen in combat locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2223 shall be assigned Exhibit P2493. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now on the same topic, if we could go to P1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as it's coming up, I'll note this is another document from the Drina Corps Command Security Department. This is 15 -- dated "15/4/1995," to the various brigades and intelligence and security organ heads, again from Chief Major Vujadin Popovic. It says "Major" in the English translation. I'm not sure that's correct, but it's -- let me just ask you about it. It's entitled "Arrest and detention of POWs and other persons, instruction." So now we have a specific reference to POWs. Let's look a bit down it. I won't read all of it. It says that: "We received a telegram, strictly confidential ..." from the VRS Security administration which outlines procedures during the detention or arrest of persons violating rules and regulations, and says that: "We submit to you the instructions in full." And it says: "Inform military police units with the instruction and act upon the provisions listed." And it begins, and I won't go through all of it, but it says: "Based on information we received, negligent behaviour has been noticed towards POWs from the moment they are captured to the moment they are taken to Batkovic collection centre or to another place of detention, as well as during detention itself." And then it says: "Namely, our soldiers often make captured enemy soldiers walk along the front-line, then take them to the command posts for interrogation. They drive them through the territory. They are held in the barracks ..." Then they're soon exchanged. So what's the basic concern in this document that led to these instructions being provided?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concern is that even though these individuals are being captured as prisoners, the way that they are being handled is exposing the prisoner to information that would be of detriment to the VRS when the individual is ultimately exchanged. The fact that an individual is a prisoner of war doesn't mean that that person is not capable of knowing where he is, ascertaining the locations of command posts or the names of individuals within those command posts, the locations of other military equipment or facilities, as part of his routine handling and processing in interrogation, and that that information would be of value to the other side when the prisoner is exchanged. So in this context, they're directing them how to modify their handling procedures, or, more accurately, how to enforce proper handling procedures so that after a prisoner is captured, he's not inadvertently afforded the opportunity to collect information sensitive to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we look at page 2 of the English - it's under paragraph 2 of the instructions in the document, so I think it's the next page in the Serbian - and I won't, again, read all of it. We can see the various things they're talking about the MPs are to do with the prisoners, and make sure they're handcuffed and their hands are tied. Then in the middle of paragraph 2, it says: "The location where POWs are collected must be such that the prisoners are fully secured, as well as the people from the security organ, from the intelligence organ and the military police organ that engages in the interrogation and guards the POWs." Does this instruction reflect the actual practice of the MPs and the security organs working in the securing of prisoners and the like?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects the fact that those particular elements are -- have various responsibilities during this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A last question. I believe it's been suggested in some of the questioning by the Defence that it was the logistics branch that had primary responsibility or significant responsibility for prisoners of war. Is that correct, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The logistics or rear services branch would have a significant role in feeding, water, life support, medical support, if necessary, to a prisoner, but the logistics branch obviously would not have the expertise necessary to interrogate a particular prisoner in that sense. I mean, again, all partners -- all sections of the military have various roles and responsibilities, so, I mean, they are a -- the logistics branch does have a role, but it certainly wouldn't be engaged in roles outside its area of competence, such as counter-intelligence or trying to gain information from a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or how about securing them, overseeing the securing and the transport of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That falls more within the competence of the military police, in so much as they would be securing the prisoners, as well as military police traffic units, which would actually organise the convoys, although, obviously, the rear services or logistics branch would provide the physical vehicles and fuel necessary to move them. It's a collaborative effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I believe we're a little past break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now, and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, 65 ter 397, that large document that you mentioned, we have picked out the relevant pages, which is now 65 ter 7453, but it's been MFI'd as P2491. So we have the relevant pages in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very good. And this one should now be received as an exhibit, I think with the same number, P2491, if there is no concern by Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: P2491 is no longer MFI'd. It's now used for the up-loaded portion of the whole document. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Staying on this topic of security and intel for now, the Drina Corps has -- as we've been going over Colonel Popovic, let's go to 65 ter 5292, which, if we just all take a look at that front page, is -- says "Analysis of Combat Readiness of the Drina Corps for Each Element of the B/G for 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Butler, briefly, what this analysis document is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a manner similar to the 1992 analysis done by the Main Staff, this is an example of an analysis done by a corps-level command. In this case, it was the Drina Corps, and it was the analysis of their work in 1994, published in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 17 in the English and page 16 in the B/C/S. This is just to get us on to the correct chapter, which should be Chapter -- I think it should be Chapter 6. As we see, the Serbian is correct. The English is wrong, in terms of the number. So that's where their section begins, and I just want to go to the next page. The B/C/S should be 16 and may catch 17 as well, and it's page 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to just ask you briefly about this paragraph. We see, in the middle of the page in the English, and it begins: "Electronic surveillance in the Drina Corps ..." And it just talks a bit about their electronic surveillance, which the Trial Chamber has heard a lot about the BiH electronic surveillance. But what I really want to ask you about is the section that says: "Intelligence data obtained by interrogating prisoners of war and defectors constitutes the main element in information about the enemy, his strength, composition, artillery support and intentions." So we see this under the intelligence and security support. Would this fit in according to the rules that you're aware of and according to the basic procedures and guide-lines that you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "The processing of prisoners of war is being approached very professionally and responsibly, with information being presented to the commands and units in whose zone of responsibility the work is being conducted." And, again, this is under the security section, working with prisoners of war. Does that conform to the rules and practices as the security organs should be involved in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this analysis, this document, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5292 shall be assigned Exhibit P2494. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now I want to change gears a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we get away from our discussion of the rules of command, security, and intel organs, and some of the practical applications, as we've seen, and get back or into the narrative of documents that relate to this area that you have reviewed and have talked about in your testimony and your narrative. And could we start with -- I believe I see it as 65 ter 29. And this, we can see, is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 19 November 1992, and it's entitled "Directive for further operations of the Army of Republika Srpska," to the commander and chief of staff personally, Directive Operational 4. Mr. Butler, is this a document you've had a chance to study and review over the years.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it says "Directive number 4." Are you aware of other directives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, to your knowledge, what are these directives? And just for everyone's knowledge, if we -- if we looked at the end of this particular directive, I believe we would see that it is drafted by General Milovanovic, but it's in the name of Commander Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic. So at this level, what are these directives? And just tell us, roughly, do you know how many there were throughout the war, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, there were a total of nine what's known as strategic directives that were issued at various points during the armed conflict. In general, what these documents are is they help define the operational context of how the political will of the RS leadership is being translated into broader military objectives. For example, you have the six strategic objectives that we've talked about previously. What you have, then, at this level of the military is more detailed planning documents which lay out, in more concrete terms, how the army intends to achieve those objectives as the conflict situation changes over various points in time. In some cases, the directive had a life of, perhaps, three or four months before it was superseded. In other cases, a directive might have been valid for a year before it needed to be superseded again, depending on the situation. So these are very strategic documents that outline the military's conduct of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we begin to -- if we leaf through this, we see that they -- it appears to go -- there's a paragraph 5 on page 4 of the English, and on page 10 or 11, but it just says: "The task of the units" and it starts with the 1st Krajina Corps, goes to the 2nd Krajina Corps, then goes to the East Bosnia Corps. So on page 5 of the English, page 11 of the B/C/S, we get to the Drina Corps. So how is -- can you explain why they go in by corps? What does this have to do with the individual corps, this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps are the highest-level combat component of the Army of the Republika Srpska. Obviously, their activities are controlled by the Main Staff, but the Main Staff is just that, it's a staff. It's not a combat command. It doesn't project combat power. That is done by the corps commands. So while the Main Staff, you know, will direct how the operations are to be done, the reality is that it will be the corps commands who will have to fight those battles and achieve those objectives in their designated zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we're at the Drina Corps, and recalling that this document is dated 19 November 1992, we look at this, and it says: "... from its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region ..." And the wider Podrinje region, would that include the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says: "... the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave Birac, Zepa and Gorazde ..." I'll stop there for a minute. Anything against the rules of the VRS or the rules, that you're aware of, of the Geneva Conventions about exhausting the enemy and inflicting the heaviest possible losses on him? Any issue you see there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to that point, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says. "... force him," meaning the enemy, "to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas ..." Do you recall this Birac area, what area that includes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Birac area would include, for example, the area of Sekovici, Western Zvornik municipality, it would include Vlasenica. It's a part of the upper Podrinje area -- I'm sorry, lower Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then this line, well: "... inflict the heaviest loss on him," meaning the enemy, "and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." How do you read that? What do you read that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it's written, it reflects the fact that not only were the military forces viewed to be a target for attack, but in this particular context, so was the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you believe the intention was towards the Muslim population, based on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to significantly reduce the Muslim population that was living in that area. At the time, even this late in 1992, the Muslim population was still the dominant population group in these various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you be more specific? When it says force him to leave these areas together with the Muslim population, what is he saying, in your view, about what to do with the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he's saying is, essentially, they want to create whatever conditions are required in order to force the Muslim population to flee from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 29 shall be assigned Exhibit P2495. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next exhibit, 65 ter 2220.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for it to come up: We'll see it's dated a few days after the last document. This is 24 November 1992, and this is from the Drina Corps Command. And if we look at the last page in English and in the Serbian, we'll see that this is in the name of the commander of the Drina Corps, Milenko Zivanovic. And this is "Decision for Further Operations," is the title, and it's to, in particular, the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade Command, personally to the commander or the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm on the first page. Excuse me. If we could -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to the top of the page, where it says: "Pursuant to Directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Strictly Confidential 02/5 of 19 November 1992, and an assessment of the situation, I have decided:" This reference, is that related to the document we just saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at the document that we just saw, which is, I guess, Prosecution Exhibit 29, we'll see Strictly Confidential 02/5, dated 19 November. Now, for some reason the document from the Drina Corps Command does not include the "-210" in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But, otherwise, do you think they're connected?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In this first sentence: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." How do you relate this sentence to the similar one where I read that talked about the Birac and Podrinje regions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically, the area that he's talking about encompasses those regions. From a command perspective, this is the corps commander taking the general guidance that he has received from the Main Staff, doing his own personal assessment, and then issuing his more detailed orders to his subordinates to implement, so it clearly reflects the fact that General -- or at that time Colonel Zivanovic, as the corps commander, you know, understands the specific intent of the broader document that -- you know, the broader guidance that's included in Directive 4 and that he's making his supplemental orders down to his brigades for implementation. This is, in a way, how the command staff process works.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this statement, "enforce the Muslim local population to abandon," these areas, based on your knowledge of the military rules that we've gone over, the laws of the Geneva Conventions that we've gone over, can there be anything legitimate in a statement in this decision by General Zivanovic to force the Muslim local population to abandon the areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the SFRY rules, and the application of those rules on the armed forces, they clearly note that, you know, civilians are not to be the objects of attacks. It's hard to square that particular regulation and application of law against this particular directive, where Colonel Zivanovic is making it clear that the intention is to force the local Muslim population to abandon their home region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this -- oh, it's P -- this document is P2434, I see, so it's already in evidence. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 688.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, we're still in 1992 and 1993, but did you look through any documents to find any outline of what may have -- what military activity may have occurred in the region just described by General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this is that we see on our screen? We see a Cyrillic picture of something.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the copy -- or that's the front cover of what is known as "Drinski" magazine, which in June of 1995 was being published on a monthly basis by the Zvornik Infantry Brigade as an informational product to the soldiers and the local municipality, promoting the activities and the members of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to B/C/S page 6. It should be page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a section in the magazine. It's entitled "Liberation of the Podrinje." Can you tell us what this is and how this fit into your narrative or your knowledge of the area, and understanding it's just a magazine?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the fact that it's just a magazine doesn't mean that it does not have information of intelligence value, which is why we looked at it first, along with other documents. But in this particular article, as it discusses the three years of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, one of the most significant military actions that the Zvornik Brigade had fought into up to date was what they called the liberation of the Podrinje or Drina Valley area. And so as part of their discussion on their unit history, they laid out in some detail what activities the unit was involved in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from your review of materials, this and others, were you able to determine whether or not there were combat actions that were taken pursuant to General Zivanovic's decision that we just saw based on -- from November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Combat actions were initiated on that, and, frankly, the first month, month and a half of combat did not go well for the Bosnian Serb military forces. It was not until February of 1993 that the military tide turned in favour of the Bosnian Serb military forces and they were able to render a number of significant military defeats on the Muslim forces in those areas and eventually force them out of large portions of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe to us -- you've talked about the military defeats. Where, if anywhere, did the civilian population that was the subject of General Zivanovic's decision -- where did those people go, those Muslims from the areas that was described by General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, the Muslim population who were in that broader area went in two different directions. Those that could, as a result of geography and when weather permitted, essentially went due west and made their way to ABiH lines near Tuzla, and effectively left that region entirely. Those individuals who were further to the south or could not, because of weather concerns, get out - it was a very bitter winter that particular winter and a lot of snow fell, causing a lot of problems - in fact went south and ultimately ended up in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your understanding of the conditions that led to the creation of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As February and March rolled -- 1993 rolled around, the Drina Corps militarily had been able to eliminate most of the Bosnian Muslim military presence north of the Konjevic Polje-Milici-Vlasenica road, that area that's generally referred to as Cerska or Erdut. They then -- as they began working their way back towards Bratunac and Srebrenica, they slowly compressed the Muslim military forces, as well as the accompanying civilian population, back into Srebrenica from the north. At the same time, there were military operations coming up the road from Skelani and the south, essentially squeezing the Muslim military forces that were left there, as well as the Muslim civilian population, into a pocket in and around the town of Srebrenica, which by then was the last stronghold of the Bosnian Muslims from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did this situation reach its peak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it reached its peak in early May -- either late April or early May, and it was when it developed into a rather large humanitarian crisis is when you saw General Morillon made his unilateral declaration of that area being a UN-protected safe area. Initially, the plan was that -- or the plan was by the VRS to try to evacuate civilians out. Approximately 8.000 of them were able to get out before that plan fell apart, when the BiH government didn't want to de-populate the area anymore, and then, under the circumstances, General Morillon felt he had no choice but to make that, you know, declared safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after Morillon's personal involvement, did the UN, itself, follow up, the Security Council, with the formal designations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, first in Srebrenica, and then supplemental declarations were made that covered Zepa and other safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are those events described, in part, in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do discuss them to a limited degree in my report. However, I think the best source of information on that I incorporated in my report is the reference, which is the United Nations' own report on the Srebrenica safe area, which I believe was published in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this 65 ter 688 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I need a clarification. We have four pages' translation into English, but many different articles in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by Mr. Registrar that only pages 8 and 9 of the original B/C/S, which are translated, should be offered and received into evidence. Is that your understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And if you see the English translation, it says "page 8 and 9," and the title is "The Third Anniversary." I believe what they've done is they've just translated that particular article on the third anniversary of the Zvornik Brigade which gave that historical background, and so that's all that we were offering in this particular segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 688 shall be assigned Exhibit P2496. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could now go to 65 ter 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we see that on the first page of this, we have a document from the Main Staff to the corps, entitled "Combat Order for the Liberation of Zepa and Gorazde." It's a long document. If we look towards the end of it, we'll see that it was drafted by Colonel Miletic, in the name of the deputy commander, General Milovanovic. Can you just -- we see that it's May 1993, around that time-period you've just spoken to. Can you just briefly put this in context? Is this something that actually happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an attempt to make it happen. What you see is very quickly, regarding Srebrenica, the VRS then attempted to move and take down Muslim military and civilian populations in Zepa and Gorazde, perhaps anticipating that they, too, at some point would be covered under some form of a safe area, and so this reflects the combat order for that. I'm not sure that -- given the timing, that significant combat activities took place, because I believe it was within a week or two that the next declaration of safe areas which will cover these two went into play. But this reflects the plan to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1979 shall be assigned Exhibit P2497. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is the end of the first binder, and it's probably a good place to stop for the night. And I will continue in the morning, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We're looking forward to the next two binders we will deal with tomorrow and perhaps after tomorrow. Indeed, we should adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow, in the morning, at 9.00 in this courtroom. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we give -- excuse me. Could we give Mr. Butler binder 2 for his review/study? It's the binder that we gave to him already, but he hasn't really been able to have it. So everyone knows what it is. I think it's binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher, he shall. And binder number 1 shall be given back to the Prosecution, I suppose. Thank you very much. The binders were exchanged. We adjourn for the day. And I have to remind you, again, please, no contact to either party about the content of your testimony during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
